EntertainmentTab.title: How 2000s lad culture helped Russell Brand to hide in plain sight
EntertainmentTab.text:
Warning: This article contains graphic descriptions of sexual acts

No British celebrity navigated the cultural changes of the early 21st Century better than Russell Brand.

His life has been one long personal rebrand.

He morphed from provocative stand-up comic to TV star and Hollywood actor. He became a YouTuber and political activist, taking up left-wing causes around issues of inequality in the 2010s, then Covid conspiracies and in 2024 supporting Donald Trump for president. That same year he was baptised as a Christian in London's River Thames.

Now he has a new persona to try on: convicted rapist.

On Thursday, the disgraced comedian was found guilty of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault at Southwark Crown Court, following a three-week trial.

As he faces jail, it's clear that the behaviour that formed the backdrop to Brand's prosecution is the same behaviour that helped elevate him in the first place.

Brand shot to fame as a sexually outrageous libertine whose risque humour thrilled audiences.

He cultivated the image of an insatiable, shameless womaniser. Sex, drugs and excess were central to his comic material.

Over the decade of his offending, Brand sold out stand-up comedy venues and theatres, broadcasters - including MTV, Channel 4 and the BBC - started to throw money at him.

With his backcombed hair and drainpipe black jeans, Brand regaled audiences at his stand-up comedy gigs with the graphic details of his sexual exploits: anal sex, prostitutes and orgies.

He simulated masturbation and sex on stage. He said he liked oral sex with women "where it goes in their neck a little bit" and their "mascara runs a little bit," acting it out on stage.

Even Brand's own barrister called the humour "a product of its time," reminding the jury in the trial that this graphic sexualised comedy was viewed as "radical and different" back then.

Barely a generation later, many will view it as deeply rooted misogyny dressed up as humour. But these were different times.

The late nineties and early noughties in Britain were an era that celebrated casual sexism and often elevated celebrities who espoused it.

In 1999, FHM projected a naked photo of the Scottish TV presenter Gail Porter on to the Houses of Parliament. She only found out when she saw it on the news, and spoke later about how it deeply affected her mental health.

What might now be termed toxic masculinity was often deemed funny, seen by some as good old-fashioned male humour. By others it was viewed as palatable because they believed it was being done with an apparently ironic eyebrow raise.

"There is no question he was a very talented stand-up," says Sarah Ditum, author of Toxic: Women, Fame and the Noughties. "There was an appetite for taboo breaking.

"I think it looks very old hat if you look back on that stuff. It's dated horribly and I don't think many people are going to be keen to defend Brand's act now knowing that it reflected his real world behaviour rather than an ironic performance."

But there were clues at the time that his outrageous stage act did not stop when the show ended - most publicly in his 2007 bestselling memoir, My Booky Wook.

"I'm a bloke from Grays with a good job and a terrific haircut who's been given a Wonka ticket to a lovely sex factory 'cos of ol' fame."

Of course, many of his sexual partners consented. As his defence barrister told the jury "he devoted himself for many years to a highly promiscuous life", reminding them that "having lots of sex is completely lawful".

My Booky Wook, which topped the Sunday Times bestseller chart for seven weeks in 2007 and sold 600,000 copies in hardback in the UK, opens with him checking into a clinic for sex addiction. He writes about going to lap dancing clubs and having "a lot" of oral sex in toilets and many threesomes.

"The rules change when you're famous. In that case two is often better than either none or one."

He writes about how an MTV PR "reminded me that I put lap dances and prostitutes on her gold card and got the hotel to give me cash on her account without her prior knowledge".

The Observer called it "a scandalous, libidinous memoir that is better written and more entertaining than any number of celebrity autobiographies that clog the shelves".

Heat said: "You come away from the book feeling like you really know - and like - the real Russell."

You can't imagine a celebrity these days writing a memoir in which he claims that at stage school a primetime actress, whom he names, "kissed me once in a corridor" and for years afterwards he'd tell people "'I had sex with her… And by sex, I mean bumming'".

But it's all told in a jokey, revelatory way, by "a bloke from Essex who likes birds with big bottoms and big boobs…. Lovely dolly-birds".

In light of his offending, writing that was celebrated for being frank, honest - and very funny - now looks anything but.

People "are willing to mistake irony and self-awareness for truth telling and trustworthiness," says Ditum. "The idea that he made these jokes about being this kind of sexual monster was supposed to convince you that he wasn't actually a sexual monster in real life."

Did normalising his behaviour allow him to hide in plain sight? Were the media companies who embraced him, the comedy venues who promoted him, the audiences who laughed at his humour, in some way complicit?

A former TV boss who didn't want to be named explained the thinking of his peers like this: "You've got this charismatic presenter who appears to be very, very good and you don't want to lose that.

"The women who were being persecuted didn't feel empowered to speak up and the few who did feel empowered might have been classed as troublemakers but certainly weren't really listened to because you didn't want to lose the star. That was the process."

Indeed, in Brand's trial, one of the complainants told the court she didn't report what had happened to her because she didn't think she would be believed in "those laddish culture times".

"It was my word against his," she said in her evidence.

Jo Caulfield, a contemporary of Brand's on the early noughties stand-up circuit, says she initially found him "utterly charming" but she sees that he was "enabled and nobody will say anything against it".

"People have people around them, promoters, assistants in TV. It's in the hierarchy of TV. If a runner [an entry-level production assistant] goes to his dressing room and he gets his knob out, it's like, 'oh, come on, don't make a fuss.'"

And while safeguarding standards have been heavily tightened in some parts of the entertainment world, she says it "still goes on".

"Nobody wants to upset the star. This person is making them money so everybody down the food chain better not say anything if they behave badly," says Caulfield.

At the end of My Booky Wook, Brand writes "I have done some terrible things over the course of this booky wook… I mean, over my life."

We now understand quite how terrible.

EntertainmentTab.title: U2 on Dolly Parton's final duet; and the 'grudge match' behind their new album
EntertainmentTab.text:
U2 are at their best when they act on instinct.

Their biggest songs are fuelled by fiery indignation (Pride, Sunday Bloody Sunday) or sudden inspiration (One, Sometimes You Can't Make It On Your Own).

When they overthink, they misfire. An attempt to marry grunge and hip-hop on the 2009 single Get On Your Boots was, in the words of drummer Larry Mullen Jr, "a catastrophic choice".

So it was a good sign when, at the start of 2026, the band rushed out two EPs of new music, ripped from the headlines of a world in turmoil.

The first, Days of Ash, was urgent and angry – addressing the shooting of US citizen Renee Good by an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer; and the death of Palestinian activist Odeh Hathaleenm, who was allegedly killed by an Israeli settler. (Yinon Levy has been charged with reckless manslaughter and said he would fight for his innocence in court.)

U2's follow-up, Easter Lily, was more reflective, asking whether faith and friendship are enough to sustain us in challenging times.

Together, they were the band's strongest material in years, combining the combustive power of their early, post-punk incarnation with the melodic sophistication they developed in the late 1980s.

"We put those EPs out without telling anyone," says Bono, the band's voluble frontman.

"Our management, our label, they all said, 'You can't do that, people won't notice'.

"And we said, 'We don't mind. It's okay not to have a big hype behind everything'.

"And it was really beautiful. The people who we wanted to notice, noticed."

For long-term U2 watchers, that's a big shift.

This is the group who described their 2000 album All That You Can't Leave Behind as the sound of four men "re-applying for the job of biggest band in the world"; and who forced 2014's Songs of Innocence into 500 million people's iTunes libraries - an epic act of overreach that Bono's been apologising for ever, external since, external.

There's no such hoopla around their new album, Carnaval de Luz, which is getting a pretty traditional roll-out for one of the world's biggest rock bands.

Sure, there's the requisite deluge of box sets and vinyl variants, a filmed concert for BBC Two, and a handful of interviews, including this one. But, more than ever, U2 want the music to speak for itself.

The album's a companion piece and a counterbalance to Days of Ash and Easter Lily. Inspired by ecstatic nights at music festivals, it rejects anxiety in favour of what Bono calls "defiant joy".

There's a stirring ballad titled If The World Is at War, We Better Not Be; while the chiming guitars of Superficiality lend an optimism to Bono's affirmation that, "the news can't break us".

"We didn't want to be dragged down by dark clouds or melancholy," explains bassist Adam Clayton.

"Our journey from the mid 1970s was about expanding freedom and opportunity for everyone: Make your own rules, pull down what wasn't useful. Now we seem to be in a period where that's under threat and under attack.

"We wanted to make the point that we didn't want our joy robbed."

During recording sessions last year, Bono told me U2 were chasing "the sound of the future". In a separate interview with Radio 2's Jo Whiley, guitarist The Edge claimed they were working on an album of "sci-fi Irish folk".

The results sure sound like U2, though.

The electronic groove of the opening track, Go (Carnaval de Luz), echoes their experimental 90s phase; while the serrated riffs of Silencio are direct descendants of 2004's Vertigo.

Parton's original lyric was about a woman trying to choose between two men but, with help from Snow Patrol's Jonny McDaid, U2 rewrote the song to address the political divisions tearing families apart.

"Brothers turn to strangers /And sons deny their name / Somebody loses either way And every heart is torn."

Parton recorded her parts in June, less than three months before she died.

"We knew she was ill, but we had no idea that it'd be her last vocal," says Bono.

"That was a real shock. A shock for us because we'd been working with her, but a shock for anyone who loves music.

"I remember I was with [R.E.M. frontman] Michael Stipe in a car when the news came in, and he actually fell down and started sobbing. He just could not believe it.

"Probably the only thing that people can agree on in the entire world right now is Dolly Parton. Whether you're gay or straight or conservative or liberal, she was ready for you to fly at her show."

Another female presence shimmers on the fourth track, The Mirror Maker, which is dedicated to Catalan superstar Rosalía. Written after witnessing her spell-binding Lux tour, Bono describes the "heavens swirling" to reveal "the re-enchantment of the world".

"Normally you have to be dead or in jail for us to write a song about you," he laughs, "but she's a feminine force field. A kind of transcendent, ecstatic musician."

He wrote the song without her knowledge, phoning the singer afterwards to timidly seek her approval.

"It could have been excruciating if she really, really hated it," he grimaces. "I'd have had to pretend it was about Santa Rosalia, a saint who lived in a cave in Italy in the 17th Century."

According to producer Jacknife Lee, The Mirror Maker went through 196 different takes before U2 were happy, suggesting they haven't entirely abandoned their perfectionist streak.

"The early sessions for this album were at times super inspiring, and then really not that good at all," admits The Edge, identifying a stubborn "stick-with-it-ness" that stops them from giving up.

"This band is absolutely relentless," agrees Bono. "It's a grudge match."

"It's the most frustrating thing," Mullen Jr adds. "I'm always reminded of how incapable I am of doing all those things that other people find easy.

"It's always been a challenge for us, and that's what makes those moments when it [works] so special. That's why you keep on chasing it, and why you stay in a band."

There's more to U2's longevity than that, though. Their line-up has remained unchanged since they first formed at Dublin's Mount Temple Comprehensive School 50 years ago. They remain friends first, and superstars second.

When we meet, in a bingo hall that hosted some of U2's formative gigs, there's a familial vibe to the whole operation.

They tease Mullen Jr for turning a hose on fans who climbed the wall of his parents' house in 1976; and chat animatedly about their musical obsessions ("every four-piece wants to be the Beatles," confesses Bono).

Those bonds have kept the band together through commercial and critical ups and downs, not to mention the life-altering injuries that forced Bono to cancel a 2010 US tour, and neck problems that prompted Mullen Jr to skip their 2023-2024 Las Vegas residency.

Doctors advised him to retire, but after a (risky) surgical intervention, he's back behind the kit – developing an entirely new playing style to avoid further damage.

Similarly, in 1998, the band taunted Chilean dictator Augusto Pinochet during a televised concert in Santiago. At the end of the night, they invited the mothers of the victims of Pinochet's 1973 coup d'état on to the stage, who took it in turns to say the names of their children into the microphone.

"It would have been way smarter and better for us to shut up," says the Edge. "But it was artistically necessary, and we just said, 'We can't not do this'."

Reflecting further on the Macklemore controversy, he adds: "We might disagree with some of the members of the pro-Palestine movement, but we absolutely agree with the fundamentals. We absolutely agree that what's going on [in Gaza] is unconscionable and that a child's life is equally valuable, no matter what their background."

The Israeli military launched a campaign in Gaza in response to an unprecedented Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, in which about 1,200 people were killed and 251 were taken hostage.

During Israel's military campaign in Gaza more than 73,780 people have been killed, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.

Mullen Jr is equally forthright about the freedom to speak out.

"We, as a band, will fight for the right to speak your mind, as long as it doesn't incite violence," he says.

"Even if we disagree with it or don't like it, nobody - no billionaire, no promoter, no owner - has the right to censor anybody.

"And they will definitely not be censoring us, ever."

Like I said: U2 are at their best when they trust their instincts.

EntertainmentTab.title: Russell Brand: Met Police boss 'wouldn't be surprised' if more allegations made about disgraced star
EntertainmentTab.text:
The head of the Metropolitan Police said he "wouldn't be surprised" if more people came forward to make allegations about entertainer and comedian Russell Brand.

On Thursday, Brand was found guilty of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault.

Met Police boss Sir Mark Rowley also told BBC Radio 4's Today programme on Friday that what he heard reported from Brand's trial at Southwark Crown Court came very close to "victim blaming".

Brand was acquitted of two other rape charges and one allegation of attempted indecent assault. The 51-year-old will be sentenced on Monday.

Speaking to the BBC, Sir Mark said that he "wouldn't be surprised if more people came forward" about Brand and said there were "two ongoing rape investigations" into him.

Brand has already been interviewed under caution in relation to those allegations.

Sir Mark praised the bravery of the women who came forward to tell their story to the police and during the trial.

"That's a real challenge for anyone having gone through something so ghastly and you have to admire them."

The head of the Met also said that whilst Brand's case "may look different because it's about celebrity, the majority of sex offending is about people abusing power", adding that victims will be believed.

"We will do everything we can to bring to justice the powerful person who is responsible for probably the most ghastly moment in your life," he said.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has also spoken about the case, seeking to explain the Labour Party's previous association with Brand, saying "it's not always the case that people know everything about people in public life".

Some within the party attempted to court Brand's support more than a decade ago, before police began investigating him.

Ed Miliband, then the Labour leader, was interviewed by Brand in the run-up to the 2015 general election.

Now foreign secretary, Miliband has since said he regrets the interview. The BBC has approached Miliband for comment.

In 2014, Burnham, then the shadow health secretary, posted in support of Brand on Twitter following allegations about the comedian's housing arrangements.

It is not clear what Burnham had been referring to in his tweet, but the previous day, The Sun claimed Brand had paid rent at a property owned by a landlord in a tax haven, while at the same time campaigning against tax avoidance.

Brand threatened to sue the newspaper and said he would give the money to victims of the Hillsborough disaster, a group Burnham has long campaigned with.

In his 2014 tweet, Burnham said it was "depressing to see media mission to discredit someone who stops playing their game" and urged Brand to "keep going".

Speaking on Friday, Burnham told the BBC: "His crimes are horrific".

"All I can say is I had no idea of the full extent of what he was doing or what he went on to do."

It was put to Sir Mark during an interview with BBC Radio 4's Today programme that Brand's defence barrister "told jurors none of the complainants had in his words 'resisted, screamed or even tried to leave'".

Sir Mark said that what he heard reported from the trial was "very close to victim blaming".

Asked whether he would support the Victim's Commissioner's call for a legal duty in the Courts and Tribunals Bill that would require judges to direct juries on rape myths and misconceptions in every rape trial.

He said he would "strongly support" such a decision, adding: "It shouldn't be possible for inaccurate statements to be made to a jury to suggest that because a rape victim didn't behave in one way that somehow undermines their case."

Brand was refused bail following his conviction on Thursday and will now spend the weekend in custody before a return to court on Monday for sentencing.

He is expected to face a substantial prison sentence.

Once the trial was over, it was reported that Brand is also facing further rape allegations made by two women and has already been questioned by officers in relation to the complaints. The Metropolitan Police said its investigation "remains ongoing".

Details in legal documents from a hearing at London's Southwark Crown Court before Brand's criminal trial began suggest that one of the women was 16 years old at the time and featured in a Channel 4 documentary.

The actor and comedian denied the allegations.

None of the women who featured in the media investigation were the complainants from Brand's criminal trial.

During a pre-trial hearing in October, Brand tried unsuccessfully to have his criminal case thrown out.

His lawyers argued that the actor and entertainer could not receive a fair trial because of the publicity following the Dispatches programme.

During the trial, Brand faced allegations from six women spanning the decade between 1999 and 2009, when he rose to fame as one of Britain's most high-profile entertainers.

The women came to court to reveal how Brand used his immense fame to force them into sexual activity.

The judge, Mr Justice Bennathan, told Brand to expect "a significant custodial term" after the verdicts were delivered.

A man who was accused of laughing while Russell Brand sexually assaulted a woman in 2009, has been asked "to step back" from his employer while they consider the verdicts.

Jack Bayles was part of his entourage in 2009 and was said to be present when one of the sexual assaults took place.

Brand had been working on a Channel 4 project when he laid his head into the groin area of a woman who was helping him at the time.

During the trial, the victim told the court Bayles and another member of Brand's staff had asked her to give the comedian a massage, and said he wouldn't continue unless she did.

Shortly after, he sexually assaulted her.

She had complained to her manager, who told the court through a statement at the trial that the victim had described how the men had laughed while the attack took place.

In recent years, Bayles has been working for the TV production company, Various Artists Ltd, as their head of comedy.

In a statement, they told the BBC: "We have asked Jack Bayles to step back from the company whilst we consider the verdict and events surrounding the trial. Our thoughts, though, are primarily with every one of Brand's victims at this time."

According to his biography on the Various Artists Ltd website, Bayles commissioned shows for Channel 4 including two series Derry Girls and Aisling Bea's This Way Up, plus Back, Year Of The Rabbit, Frank Of Ireland and Hullraisers.

In a statement, Bayles said he was sorry but doesn't remember the sexual assault.

"I am appalled and sickened by Brand's actions and have co-operated fully and voluntarily with the investigation and endeavoured to assist as best I can," he said.

"However, I do not remember the incident that took place 17 years ago in 2009. But I acknowledge that I clearly missed something at the time and did not see nor recognise that it caused distress. For that I am sincerely sorry."

Bayles said at the time of the offence he was in the early stages of his career, calling it "a frantic, pressured and toxic working environment".

He described Brand as someone who was "chaotic, dismissive and manipulated the people around him".

Bayles said this was why he decided to stop working with Brand in 2010 and had not had any contact with him since. He added that during his time with Brand, no complaints were made about the entertainer's behaviour.

"I am unaware if any were raised to anyone else more senior to me," he said.

"I would never willingly or proactively wish to make anyone feel uncomfortable, unsafe or unsupported at work. If I was ever present when Brand acted inappropriately and I failed to spot it and step in, then I sincerely apologise".

EntertainmentTab.title: Pyre: Indian film on elderly couple's love and loneliness won 18 awards - now it's wowing audiences
EntertainmentTab.text:
A film about the tender love and quiet loneliness of an elderly couple, which took two years to reach cinemas after it was completed, is wowing critics and audiences across India.

The 111-minute Pyre, directed by television journalist-turned-filmmaker Vinod Kapri, also explores the pressing issue of outmigration which has left hundreds of picturesque Himalayan hamlets abandoned and turned them into ghost villages. It further reflects on the impact of climate change, which has made the region's weather increasingly harsh.

On social media, many Indians have shared videos showing audiences leaving theatres with tears in their eyes. Others have posted that they have not been so moved by a film in a long time.

The film's lead actors, ordinary villagers who had never faced a camera before, have also won praise from some of Bollywood's most respected figures, including Naseeruddin Shah and Anupam Kher.

Pyre's protagonists - Padam Singh (played by Kapri's uncle, Padam Singh) and Tulsi (played by Heera Devi) - are Bubu and Aama, local terms for grandfather and grandmother. The couple live in a small home in the mountains of the northern state of Uttarakhand .

It's a place where age is measured against momentous events. Singh was born two years before the outbreak of World War II. Tulsi was born in the year atomic bombs were dropped on Japan.

There are no roads and no electricity. Whenever the couple need help – which is often as Tulsi frequently has to be carried to hospital – Padam Singh uses a traditional long-horn instrument to summon neighbours. In return for their kindness, he pays them with goats.

"There's nothing here – just mountains," as one character puts it. So the young leave in search of greener pastures, and those who depart this beautiful, but blighted, land rarely return.

Kapri says his film remains focused on the "soulful love story of the ageing couple in their last days".

"They have shared a life together for 65 years and, for the last 28 years, they've been waiting for their son, Hariya, who's gone to Mumbai in search of work, to come back," Kapri tells the BBC. "It's a story of companionship, of loneliness and of waiting."

Their wait takes on a new urgency when suddenly, after all these years, a letter arrives from Hariya setting a date for his visit.

As Padam Singh and Tulsi count down the days, the handful of villagers around them leave one by one, until the couple find themselves alone in the vast mountain landscape.

"You and Tulsi should also leave as soon as possible. Otherwise, you won't even have four people to carry your body down the mountain to the funeral pyre when you or Tulsi die," one departing villager advises Padam Singh. "Or die before we leave," he adds in jest.

With no one left to call for help, Padam Singh builds two funeral pyres side by side right outside his door – one for his wife and one for himself.

"How will I carry you down the mountain if you die?" he tells Tulsi when she questions the decision.

Despite the bleak setting and the weight of the topics covered, Pyre is suffused with humour. The central couple are delightful. Like many long-married spouses, they seem to treat bickering as a love language.

Kapri, who is from Uttarakhand, got the idea for the film in 2018 after meeting an 84-year-old man in Munsiyari, a scenic hill town in the state.

"I visited him after seeing his photo in a Facebook post. The wrinkles on his face really fascinated me. His face was unique."

Kapri said he asked him and his wife what their biggest worry was.

"He said, 'My biggest worry is, if I die first, who is going to take care of her?' And she said, 'He doesn't know how to cook. So if I die first, I don't know who is going to cook food for him.' That was so heartwarming for me."

Kapri says he initially tried to make his film with "the real couple", but abandoned the idea after a week of shooting, when it became clear it was not working. He then approached actors Naseeruddin Shah and Ratna Pathak - a couple themselves - for the lead roles.

Shah loved the script, Kapri says, but felt that he and Pathak did not belong to the region and would struggle to do justice to the characters.

Kapri finally found his Padam Singh within his own family – his father's younger brother, a retired army soldier who expressed an interest in acting. He found his Tulsi in another village. Heera Devi, an elderly widow, had raised her children through years of farming, cutting grass and tending to her buffalo.

They have met teary-eyed people at multiple screenings - many wanting to touch their feet and hug them, many who said the film reminded them of their own parents and grandparents who are waiting in villages, towns and cities that they had come from.

"We felt immense joy and happiness. We've received so much love and inspiration - something we had never imagined," says Padam Singh.

But the best moment for him came when he met Naseeruddin Shah in Mumbai. "He watched the entire movie and had tears in his eyes. He hugged me. He said, 'Bubu, the role you have performed, I wouldn't be able to pull off even in seven lifetimes.'"

The film's appeal, Heera Devi says, is because "in reality, our village is just like this".

"Across villages in India, the elderly are left alone. No one's children stay at home anymore and it's the same situation for all parents. They keep waiting for their son and daughter-in-law, hoping that their grandchildren would visit and spend a few days with them. The loneliness is simply unbearable."

Padam Singh says he has a message for the younger generation in Uttarakhand and the rest of India.

"I want to tell them they must not abandon their motherland, the land where they were born," he says. "I also appeal to the government to bring education and employment to where people are - so that they don't have to wander away. When that happens, the parents who are being left behind will also be cared for."

The 111-minute Pyre, directed by television journalist-turned-filmmaker Vinod Kapri, also explores the pressing issue of outmigration...

EntertainmentTab.title: Olivia Rodrigo's Christmas song sounds familiar... on purpose
EntertainmentTab.text:
Pop star Olivia Rodrigo unwrapped her first-ever Christmas song on Thursday night, alongside a festive music video starring Sex and the City star Cynthia Nixon.

The track, called Take Me Home (4 Christmas), finds the pop star asking her boyfriend to "show some serious commitment" by bringing her to his parents' house for the Christmas break.

As soon as it was released, fans noticed similarities to The Waitresses' 1981 festive hit Christmas Wrapping... And it turns out that was by design rather than mistake.

Chris Butler, who wrote The Waitresses' song, posted a message on Facebook, external, saying Rodrigo had contacted him to seek permission for the song; and praising her "phenomenal" writing.

"About two months ago, I received a weird email from someone claiming to be 'Olivia Rodrigo'," he said. "Said she'd written a Christmas song, and invited me to hear it."

Admitting he'd never heard of the pop star before, Butler said he assumed the email was a fake.

But after researching her career, he became a fan - not just of her music, but of the fact she'd hired an all-female band, and negotiated control of her master recordings.

In the end, he decided to reply to her email - and posted the text to his Facebook profile.

"If you really are you, thanks for contacting me. And your comments are really sweet, and very flattering," he said.

"They're really sweet and flattering... even if you AREN'T you.

"If you really are Olivia Rodrigo: I like you, I like your music. I like the arrangements especially. Soft-loud-soft, etc. And that your recordings sound like people are playing on them.

He continued: "I like that your lyrics are intense, real, and poetic. I like that you "got" my songwriting, and that you like our band."

Butler also accepted the invitation to hear Rodrigo's Christmas song, and told his followers: "Her song was/is great.

"It's going to be a smash, maybe even that elusive Christmas number one contest they have every year in the UK."

Although the song is indebted to the Waitresses' new wave and post-punk sound, Butler does not receive a writing credit on Take Me Home (4 Christmas) as it neither samples nor interpolates any of his music.

Posting on social media, Rodrigo said it was written last summer with her longtime collaborator Dan Nigro, and Amy Allen, who has previously contributed to songs by Harry Styles, Sabrina Carpenter and Tate McCrae.

Meanwhile, the Christmas jumper-tastic video, external follows the single's storyline, with SNL star Ben Marshall playing her feckless boyfriend, and Nixon starring as her prospective mother-in-law.

EntertainmentTab.title: 1Xtra launches first ever UK rap chart for 'fair playing field'
EntertainmentTab.text:
British rap artists will step into the spotlight later when BBC Radio 1Xtra launches the first ever dedicated rap chart based on UK listening figures.

DJ Kenny Allstar, who'll host the countdown on Friday nights, has one word: "Finally".

"If we have our own fair playing field where we can all be celebrated... it then feels fair and it feels exciting," he tells BBC Newsbeat.

Currently artists compete across genres for a spot in the Official Singles Chart, but Allstar says this is dominated by pop music, making it harder for other genres to be heard.

Perhaps with the exception of heavyweights like Central Cee and Dave, who broke chart records with Sprinter back in 2023, "it's not easy for any artist to go against Sabrina Carpenter and Taylor Swift every week," he says.

Compiled by the Official Charts Company, 20 rap singles from British artists will be ranked each week based on streams and sales in the UK.

It follows the launch of other genre-specific charts including for R&B, 'homegrown' albums and British Asian music.

Allstar hopes it'll give UK rap a boost as he acknowledges it has taken a bit of a beating recently with prominent artists like Skepta and Digga saying the quality of music coming from the scene has dipped.

"I want to find solutions," he says.

"Future broadcasters and talent will benefit from this forever, I'm super gassed."

Allstar has long been a champion of UK rap and currently presents the Rap Show on BBC Radio 1, which he describes as "the show I always wanted as a kid".

This new role is "a pinch me moment," he says.

The Official Charts Company previously listed the 40 top selling R&B and hip hop tracks on its website, but there had been nowhere for fans to listen to the chart.

"It was literally just a bunch of numbers and text, so it kind of existed but not in this capacity," Allstar says.

Each week will likely see at least three or four new artists in the chart, giving emerging talent a chance to be heard by hundreds of thousands of listeners.

"What we can finally have is UK rap having its dedicated space where artists can just be celebrated," he says.

Eric Hunter, from the Official Charts Company, says the countdown will be "an amazing opportunity to shine a light on more artists, document the culture and give emerging talent a way to track their progress alongside their peers".

The company says UK rap is "one of the country's most influential and fast-moving music scenes" and the chart will celebrate both established names and the next generation of rappers driving the scene.

The debut show coincides with Skepta's long-awaited sixth studio album and Allstar says he expects to see the rapper feature in the chart.

"It's looking promising, but the only way you can find out is if you listen in," he says.

The Official UK Rap Chart will broadcast on 1Xtra each Friday from 22:00-23:00 and will be available after on BBC Sounds.

EntertainmentTab.title: RuPaul's Drag Race UK crowns winner as BBC axes the series
EntertainmentTab.text:
Warning: This article includes spoilers for the finale of RuPaul's Drag Race UK.

After 10 weeks of toe-to-toe lip-syncs, fierce runways and shady remarks, the time has come for one queen to be named the UK's next Drag Race superstar.

For the final time on the BBC, 12 contestants were whittled down to just one after the broadcaster announced it was axing RuPaul's Drag Race UK due to budget cuts.

On Thursday night, RuPaul crowned Flesh as the series eight winner.

The London queen snatched the title from Mocha, Naya Thorn and Alik, who also made it to the final episode.

The 26-year-old was crowned by last year's winner, Bones, who is also her best friend and drag sister, with the duo performing together as Heavenly Bodies.

Speaking to BBC Newsbeat after celebrating overnight, the Soho queen says the win still feels "surreal" and she spent the whole evening "smiling, crying, and laughing".

She will be the last queen crowned on the BBC before the UK edition moves to Wow Presents Plus, a streaming platform owned by the production company behind the show.

While some fans have welcomed the prospect of a new chapter for the series which might include bigger cash prizes, like in other spin-offs, others fear leaving the BBC will mean less representation for LGBTQ+ culture.

Flesh says the move to Wow could widen the range of performers and subcultures featured on the show, but worries the shift to subscription could reduce the audience for drag.

"This is where it feels slightly sadder that we're leaving the BBC because for all of the parameters that it created that limited what we could do, there was more exposure than drag has ever been given," she says.

She admits she is "concerned" about the "knock-on effect" this could have on the future of the UK drag industry, such as creating fewer opportunities for contestants.

"Without that exposure, there will be less demand and with less demand and less exposure, events won't be able to be created," she says.

Amid this concern, Flesh encourages people to connect with their local drag community and performers to consider ways they can evolve performances to bring in new audiences.

The decision to shelve the programme was announced shortly after the latest series began airing, with the BBC saying it was facing "very difficult choices" amid "significant financial pressures".

Flesh was awarded the £25,000 cash prize after impressing the judges in the final maxi challenge, which saw the last four queens perform a megamix of girl group anthems from past series.

Wrapping the show's stint on the BBC this way felt like a "really fun and tasteful way to reflect on the iconography of Drag Race UK", says Flesh, who hopes the past contestants feel "honoured".

But she reveals the final group of queens did think the "writing was on the wall" for show's future when they were asked to do the mix.

Flesh has stood out across the series as a fashion queen, bringing looks to the runway that RuPaul said would go down in the series' history.

Speaking to RuPaul and judge Michelle Visage during the final episode, Flesh said Drag Race "tells people it's not only OK to be them but it's a gift and a dream, and to be crowned the UK's next drag race superstar would be mine coming true".

She made it through the series without ever being in the bottom two and only had to lip-sync for the first time in the final when the top three queens battled it out for the win.

After Alik was eliminated, Flesh, Mocha and Naya Thorn performed a rendition of David Bowie's Modern Love.

EntertainmentTab.title: ‘Life is like a heartbeat. It’s up and down, up and down’: Michelle Yeoh on casting cliches, marriage at 60 and playing a robot in Blade Runner 2099
EntertainmentTab.text:
Before agreeing to appear in Blade Runner 2099, Michelle Yeoh received a letter – “an amazing letter, a love letter” – from Silka Luisa, the project’s creator, imploring her to be involved. Yeoh, who is 64, has played grandes dames, action heroes and a low-income Chinese-American battling the tax authorities in an infinite multiverse, but Blade Runner was different. The sci-fi series, a follow-up of sorts to Ridley Scott’s 1982 movie classic and its 2017 sequel, features both humans and replicants, their bioengineered antagonists, and Yeoh was adamant: “I don’t want to be human.” After working on ideas of what a synthetic human might look like, the result is Olwen, a terrifying individual with “a very cold, steely look in her eyes. And the way she moves – it’s not robotic. She’s sort of fluid. Like a dragon. Like a serpent.”

Yeoh is an actor who likes to figure things out for herself and, in the prep stages for Blade Runner 2099, the key question she thought about while building her character was, “What is it to be human? Are you born with humanity or does it come from the things you go through?”

Appearing via video link from New York, Yeoh exudes high-energy enthusiasm in plain white T-shirt, scraped back hair and huge, dark-framed glasses, all of which give her a cheerful, just-out-of-rehearsal air. She talks a mile a minute – about her family, the show, her holiday last summer on Luc Besson’s island in the Bahamas – and if her exuberance comes as a mild surprise, it’s because in recent years, much of Yeoh’s acting has been characterised by stillness. Her roles as Eleanor Young, the icy matriarch in the 2018 hit movie Crazy Rich Asians, and the crushed figure of Evelyn Wang, owner of a failing laundromat in Everything Everywhere All at Once (for which she won an Oscar in 2023, the first Asian woman to win for best actress), turn on tiny facial adjustments and furious or haughty looks, suggesting a performer who favours the minimalist approach.

As fans of Yeoh will know, however, the actor started out as a dancer, moved to martial arts movies in the 80s and is as robustly physical as any in Hollywood. An action star at heart, Yeoh is quick on her feet and unprecious in her outlook – so much so that, on occasion, she has found Hollywood a bit cautious compared with the wild west of the Hong Kong film industry she came up in as a young woman. “I’m tiny, I’m petite, five foot four,” she says, yet her ability to change her affect through movement is so intense, so persuasive, that, placed alongside Hunter Schafer, her much taller co-star in Blade Runner, “somehow you feel I loom over her”.

Schafer plays Cora, Yeoh’s sidekick Blade Runner – that is, a replicant cop with the LAPD – tasked with bringing a missing colleague back to base. The story’s complicating factors are that Cora is a human pretending to be a replicant, and Yeoh’s character, Olwen, is staring down her own imminent, preprogrammed death. The show is set 50 years after the last instalment of the Blade Runner franchise, in a world in which the replicants are running things and humans occupy a permanent serf-class. It’s chillingly timely, given recent instances of AI slipping its reins, and the challenge for Yeoh, she says, went beyond existential questions about what it means to be human into the practicalities of how to present a character created in a lab. “They had no childhood,” she says, “so you feel you’re dealing with someone who has no concept of private space. They’re in your face and if they want something, they take it. With Olwen, I wanted it so you don’t know where she is or what she’s going to do next, and everyone is terrified.”

Yeoh’s own childhood, in a middle-class Malaysian Chinese family, was one in which her ambitions, intellectual and professional, were broadly encouraged. Her father, Datuk Yeoh Kian-teik, was a prominent lawyer and businessman who had trained in England and her mother, Janet, a former beauty queen who would have an enormous influence on Yeoh’s career. In some ways, it was a highly conventional background, and when Yeoh expressed a desire to pursue dance as a career, her parents thought it entirely suitable that “I’d learn my ballet, graduate as a teacher, then come home and start my own ballet school. They were happy.”

In other ways, however, her background was more interesting and diverse than the average. The city she grew up in, Ipoh, is the capital of a Malaysian state 200km north of Kuala Lumpur and was a thriving, cosmopolitan place. This somehow made the world appear more accessible and when, at 15, she won a place to study ballet at the Hammond school in Chester, it made her decision to leave home so young seem less outlandish.She says she travelled, unaccompanied, to England, where she had plenty of cousins, but it remains surprising that her family permitted her not only to cross the world alone, but to live in student accommodation 7,000 miles away.

Yeoh says these kinds of ambitions were built into her upbringing. “I was always a bit of an adventurer, which my parents instilled in us. My dad has a philosophy that education is precious, but you can decide what you want to do. He never said I had to do the big five: lawyer, doctor, accountant, that kind of thing.”

At that point, Yeoh had no desire to be an actor; her sights were set on performing in ballet. It has been an interesting facet of her life and career that she has been able to absorb sudden changes of fortune; to pivot to new experiences with relative ease. Her energy, it seems to me, is primarily playful, whether she is flying through the air in Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon or swishing her ankle-length trenchcoat as a replicant in Blade Runner. (“They are almost naughty,” she says, of the non-humans, “like something playing with its food.”)

As a result, when Yeoh’s performance becomes still, it has a particular power. There is a scene in the Blade Runner 2099 pilot in which Yeoh’s character is informed she must go after and eliminate an old replicant with whom she was close and who has apparently gone rogue. Olwen stares silently at her superior, before saying, “I have never killed one of my own.” And in that moment of stillness, a muscle in her cheek twitches. It’s a remarkable piece of acting, discreet as a poker tell. How on earth, I ask, did she do it? Yeoh smiles, glittering. “Years of practice, my dear. Years and years.”

The experiences in England set up a great fork in the road for Yeoh, who had to tear up her plans and start again. While at the school, she injured her back and was told dancing professionally was out of the question. She compares that moment to looking in a “mirror that shatters … as a silly 17-year-old, it was the end of my dream.” Looking back, she feels lucky to have been in the care of the principal, Mrs Hammond, “an older, wiser lady who said, ‘Calm down, crazy little girl. It’s not the end of the world! You can still be involved in dance.’” Accordingly, after doing A-levels, Yeoh went to what is now Manchester Metropolitan University to study for a degree in creative arts, with an emphasis on dance’s history and choreography. “At the end of the day, if that’s my next best choice, I’ll take it!”

Yeoh makes the bounce-back sound easy. Surely she had a big crash somewhere in there? She insists that, after the initial shock, she quickly rationalised her way into her former state of cheerfulness, telling herself that, after all, the new degree course “still involved the world I loved … And now when I look back, those experiences actually helped me doing martial arts.”

As a child, she had been a real jock, a champion squash player and an athlete. “I ran, I did high jump, I love the outdoors, the physical challenge. All of which helped with action movies.” That pivot was a few years off, however, and after her degree Yeoh moved home to Malaysia and wondered what to do next. She thought of opening a dance school with a friend, but her mother had other ideas. Behind Yeoh’s back – “The number of things she has done behind my back is countless” – Janet sent headshots of her daughter to the judging panel for Miss Malaysia, a competition Yeoh ended up winning in 1983 at 21. She went along with it “to get her off my back”, but when invited to compete at a further beauty contest in Australia, Yeoh put her foot down. “I said, no, I’m not doing it, I’m going back to England.”

Why not seize the opportunity to travel? Because, while “I love dancing on stage, I don’t love speaking on stage. I panic, I’m sweating, my knees are shaking. Going to Comic Con is scary as hell. I always think I’m going to make a fool of myself.” Still, Janet’s will was greater and off she went to Australia, which was just as well: the exposure brought Yeoh to the attention of a TV station in Hong Kong looking for fresh, Chinese-language acting talent. She jumped at the opportunity and landed in a strange and “terrifying” situation.

Yeoh is fond of pointing out she’s adventurous, but this was something else: finding herself cast in a movie in a language in which she wasn’t entirely fluent and couldn’t read at all. “I still can’t. Fortunately at that time in Hong Kong they didn’t have much of a script,” she says, laughing, and in the early days of filming titles such as Yes, Madam!, a cop thriller, and the action comedy The Owl vs Bumbo, she would be fed lines by the assistant director and simply repeat what she’d heard. The turnaround time on these films was phenomenal: “I remember one where we finished shooting on Monday morning after filming all night, and by Friday night it was in the cinemas. They’re editing as they go along.”

It was a speed that suited Yeoh: “It toughens you up and makes you think on your feet. It’s like being in a standup show.” As her martial arts skills improved, she swiftly became a star, churning out title after title until she met the billionaire businessman Dickson Poon. He hired her to star in a commercial for one of his ventures and within a few years they were married.

Yeoh has spoken about this marriage as an amicable failure that lasted four years, her divorce in 1992 freeing her up to return to acting; while married to Poon, she stopped working, a hangover from the more conservative elements of her background, and not something she repeated with her second husband. For the past 22 years, she has been in a relationship with Jean Todt, former head of Ferrari, whom she met in 2004 and was engaged to for 19 years before marrying in 2023. Todt has told her it was love at first sight, when he saw her “walking down some steps in Shanghai in 2004”. The pair went on to meet in Paris, for a while maintaining a long-distance relationship. (Todt, now 80, needed his friends’ help “teaching him how to text” to sustain this.) “I really liked the guy,” Yeoh says. “Very straightforward, honest, all that.” Two months after meeting, Todt proposed and, as “we got on very well”, she accepted.

Why marry at all, after such a long engagement? It was Covid, she says, that finally shunted them over the line: during lockdown, they realised Yeoh, a Malaysian passport holder, had no automatic right to travel to see Todt at their home base in Switzerland unless they were married. They tied the knot there before she took off again to film Blade Runner in Prague, Avatar 4 in the US and forthcoming movie The Surgeon in Ireland.

The hiatus taken by Yeoh during her first marriage didn’t harm her career; quite the opposite. Returning to the Hong Kong cinema scene, her celebrity rose over the next five years as the industry exploded, until, in 1997, she caught the eye of Hollywood casting directors hiring for a new Bond movie. As her first American film, this was the turning point for Yeoh, although in the first instance her experiences on the set of Tomorrow Never Dies – in which she played Wai Lin, the Chinese intelligence agent and martial artist who teams up with Pierce Brosnan to bring down Jonathan Pryce’s media mogul – were bafflingly slow compared with the world she was used to. Worse, she was prohibited from doing even the simplest of stunts. “I was an established action hero, and the first thing the director said was, you are not here because you know how to do action. You are here because you are an actress. We don’t want you to get hurt.” On the first day of filming, Yeoh was scripted to jump less than a foot down a step and to her amazement was told she wasn’t allowed to. “I’d say, are you guys pulling my leg?” But they weren’t. When the producers hired her stunt team to fly in from Hong Kong, they were amazed to be sent models of the set with which to plan their scenes. One day, as Yeoh walked past the green room, she was horrified to see them lying down. She went off: “What the hell?! They bring you all the way here and you’re lying around! Go and work!” They told her they’d already presented six options to the producers and had time for a nap because the Hollywood machine was so slow.

In the wake of Bond, a less confident actor might have felt caught between two cinematic cultures. Not Yeoh. “I never compared the two by thinking this side or that is better.” She did, however, have strong feelings about the amount of garbage she was offered after, when American cinema had no idea what to do with an Asian star. For two years she didn’t work, “not for the lack of offers” but because all the scripts that came in were “very stereotypical Asian roles”. The question a casting director or producer would ask before offering her a role, she says, was “‘Why is an Asian face in this room? Are we in Chinatown?’ There weren’t that many roles that had anything to say. I was fortunate, because I already had a very strong career in Hong Kong that had saved me enough money to have the power to say no. I didn’t want to endorse the stereotypes of our culture.”

What broke the drought and changed Yeoh’s fortunes again was being cast, in 1999, in Ang Lee’s Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon, as Yu Shu Lien, a master warrior and skilled martial artist. The film was a huge success, grossing more than $200m worldwide and proving, she laughs, that “Americans do know how to read subtitles”.

Since then, Yeoh says, the issue of racial stereotyping in casting has fluctuated wildly. For a while, “looking east was fun. It was exciting. And we had Quentin Tarantino, who liked the movies that came out of Asia, which made a big difference. Then Jackie Chan came, Jet Li, Chow Yun-fat, and the directors – John Woo, Tsui Hark, Johnny Chu. They pushed open the doors. But still they were regarded as ‘Chinese’ directors. Not quite there, yet. And it’s taken a long time.”

What moved the needle, she believes, was John M Chu’s Crazy Rich Asians, based on the bestselling novel by Kevin Kwan, which tells the story of an American Chinese girl who falls in love with the son of a billionaire. The action unfolds in Singapore and features an entirely Asian cast – a first for a mainstream US romantic comedy – in which Yeoh reigned supreme as the hero’s icy and terrifyingly elegant mother-in-law, Eleanor Young. The fact it was a huge hit, Yeoh says, “really changed things”.

Since its release, Yeoh has been cast in movies across every genre, from Star Trek to Minions to her turn in the Agatha Christie adaptation A Haunting in Venice, and as Madame Morrible in Wicked. Her greatest performance in the last five years was as Evelyn Wang, the put-upon matriarch of a failing laundromat – and other iterations in a series of alternative universes – in the indie film Everything Everywhere All at Once. Acting is so nebulous, I wonder if winning the Oscar confirmed something in her mind? “I know what you mean – life is like a heartbeat; it’s up and down, up and down. So you reassure yourself it’s OK, you did your best, but there’s never any guarantee. Any award, especially the Oscar, is a confirmation from your peers. When we started out with Everything Everywhere, we just wanted to tell a story people could understand, in the language of the younger generation, and that’s why it was so fearless. Because an older person would look at it and say, what is that? What are you smoking? Or whatever.”

It’s characteristic that, when presented with the script by directors Daniel Kwan and Daniel Scheinert, known as the Daniels, Yeoh did not have this killjoy recoil. Quite the opposite; her first thought was, “It’s so relatable, because it’s about a family in America dealing with things we all understand so well. Tax. The generation gap. Miscommunication. Love and family.”

It’s about something else, too, a more esoteric theme Yeoh perhaps understands better than most. It happened to her as a teenager, a reluctant beauty queen, and when she left Hong Kong for America, so when she encountered the notion in the Daniels’ script, with its description of a multiverse in which all versions of our lives take place simultaneously, she knew what they were saying, “that every time you make a decision, things change”. And if all the alternative futures evaporate in that moment, that is perfectly fine with Michelle Yeoh.

EntertainmentTab.title: Narrative threads: How to write a Booker-shortlisted novel, by Marlon James, Douglas Stuart, Elizabeth Strout and more
EntertainmentTab.text:
Who knows where a novel really comes from? I spend years gathering loose threads and then, when I feel like the cloth will hold, I start to weave them into a narrative. I suppose I began internalising John of John back in 1994, the year I went to college and chose to become a weaver myself.

But it was in 2019, in the anxious period waiting for Shuggie Bain to be published, that I really found the thread for John of John. I decided I would go to the Western Isles. It was a place I had been longing to see all my life and I had a vague idea that I might set a novel there about an adult son who has been called home to a crofting community to care for his difficult father. I reasoned that even if a novel didn’t emerge from the trip, at least I would have seen more of my own country.

I was drawn to the Western Isles for many reasons. I was keen to see the Harris tweed weavers, but I’d also just finished writing Young Mungo, a novel about sectarian violence where young Glaswegians seemed intent on destroying beauty, and so without being able to articulate it, I had set out seeking a spirit of gentleness, to write about creativity within working-class lives – about beauty, and colour, and nature, and music.

People have a romantic notion of the islands – and perhaps I had a little too. Although they are stunning, they are very real, very practical places, where it can be difficult to earn a living and raise a family, where managing your relationship within a community is of the utmost importance.

I started in Vatersay and, after slowly travelling up the archipelago, I finally arrived on the Isle of Harris. It was there, in the home of a local woman, that I saw what my third novel might become.

We were sitting at her kitchen table, talking about her involvement in the local church. I mentioned that I’d been struck by the number of spinsters and bachelors I’d met on my trip. It seemed unusual given that crofts seemed to benefit from larger families. When I asked her why she thought some folk had never married, she replied that they had probably just “missed their moment”. I agreed that it must be tricky to find love in a settlement with so few people, and then I ventured that it would be harder still if some of these older people had been gay. The woman looked at me with such cool horror that I realised, in that moment, that the novel was going to be less about a son returning home, and more about the father he had left behind; a weaver who was tied to the land, a man who had never been able to find love, or any sense of himself, in the only place where he belonged.

Elizabeth StroutThe Things We Never Say

A woman works in the drugstore in the town in which I live in Maine, and one day almost two years ago, she whispered to me – no one else was in the store – “I just want it over!” She cupped both hands on the sides of her mouth and said: “The election.” I told her I felt the same. She said, looking around nervously: “I never, ever say anything about it to anyone, but I just want it over.” I told her I knew what she meant, and off I went. I have no idea who she voted for, but her pain was palpable. As was mine.

The Things We Never Say is a tribute to people such as her, people who are distressed about the way things are, and have been for a few years, in our country, the United States of America. We live it, breathe it, it is everywhere among us, and while people will talk to like-minded people (sometimes) there is much that people will not say to each other about our current situation.

Not only was this true as I was writing the book, it is even more true now; the book shows the decline of our democracy. And through it all we continue living our daily lives. We go to work, we shop for groceries, we take walks with friends and laugh, we go to our quilting clubs, and all around us terrible things are happening, and most of us are not talking about it.

I have spoken publicly about my inspiration for Artie Dam, the protagonist, how I found an old photo in an obituary and saw a splendid ordinary face … This is all true, and it gave me the visuals I needed for him, but the book itself came forth because of what is happening in our country. I made Artie a high school history teacher because he would have had – perhaps – a deeper understanding of what was going to happen, and in fact, has happened.

I interwove his personal story – because we all have a personal story as we move through our time in history – and I wanted his inner life to somehow reflect what was happening in his outer life. Artie’s time in history has caught up with him, and this is his story. It is our story.

There is a blind man in Mallorca who could tell this story better than I could. What he might not have in art he has in truth, and he could tell you about his life before he went blind, his hopes when he still lived in Jamaica, the night that took his vision, the mob that nearly took his life, and the last thing he saw: the man who took his eyes out. All alleged of course. The blind man was gay – is gay – and the last thing he saw was what Jamaican men do to gay people. But until three years ago I thought this man the stuff of urban legend, a story that shook my young gay self down to the bone and sent me hurling into the closet with the door slammed shut.

The thing is I knew it happened. The rumour was that on a night in the early 90s, a mob descended on a group of gay men in Kingston, gathered at either a support group or a branch of Jamaica Aids support, and beat them within an inch of their lives. That among the mob was law enforcement, men in business and a very famous musician. All alleged, of course. There has never been a written record of it, no police report, no news article, no lead in the nightly news, and so I was convinced it happened.

Rumours are ephemeral, which is why in Jamaica they are almost always true. We know that you pay a price for standing on fact. Espousing a truth means making yourself a target. Speaking truth to power in the end attracts power to stop it. Because it is the kind of news that fades, the kind of news that is untraceable, the rumour speaker knows that he has the safety of knowing that his truth will never come back to expose or convict him. So, he speaks it freely. They killed a gay man. One of the mob was Jamaica’s biggest reggae singer. The gay men were getting safe sex advice. The gay men might have been having sex. The men were all black. The men were a mix of black and white. The men all had Aids. All alleged of course.

I tend to make novels out of stories that haunt me. The stories that haunt the most sometimes tell me the least, leaving me with gaps and leaps, and holes that stop the tale from adding up. This is where I feel most useful as a novelist; as something between a historian and a journalist, making real the lives of imagined people. Or filling in the other dimensions of a one-dimensional event. Or, most importantly, conjuring what might have been the consequences of a singular, sometimes forgotten action. It might not be exactly as the blind man in Mallorca would tell it, or it might be totally different. But a story can be real if not factually true, and sometimes that is truer than reality itself.

May We Feed the King

Poetry had left me and I missed writing. Bolstered by publishing a short work of creative nonfiction about my childhood as a competitive trampolinist, I started working on two separate short stories, testing if fiction was something I could do.

One story was about a young attendant to a dying king, and another about a lonely woman using replica food in her home to create scenes and their resident spirits, with the ultimate goal of cohabiting with them. At a point it became clear to me that she was working her way towards the young attendant, and that I was writing one book and not two separate stories at all.

A year or so before that I said to two of my friends, while visiting the Royal Magdalene Almshouses in Glastonbury and feeling transported by one of the dressed bedrooms, that I was interested in writing about staging and replica.

Thirty years before that I squeezed a plastic grape in a sofa showroom.

I had no idea what would happen in the book when I started writing it, or how it would end. Iris Murdoch once said, “One should sit quietly and let the thing invent itself”, and I took that as a mantra, letting the book emerge. It turns out that can be quite messy, and it took a while to find its final form. Initially the chapters were alternately contemporary and historical. At one point I cut and rewrote half of it. Some decisions, like the short chapters, were instinctive. Others were the work of much stylistic experimentation. All the usual messy business (I assume, having only done it once) of writing a novel.

On that journey, what surprised me most was that the wider world fed more into the writing of the medieval part of the book than it did the present-day sections. I was already thinking about power and empire, but writing at the height of the genocide in Gaza and watching in horror the results of unchallenged, untethered absolute power, certainly shaped the writing of the king and many of the characters around him. Before this, I assumed that novels exist in a state of purity in the mind, untouched by current events. I’m sure that’s sometimes true, but in my case the contemporary and medieval worlds had to be in conversation.

It was March 2021, and I had chronic neck and back pain from spending eight hours a day teaching on Zoom during the lockdowns. I was also temporarily head of my department (which anyone in academia will know to be a completely thankless and enervating role). I had given myself a night off to work on some poems because I go absolutely spare when I’m not writing. It was about 10pm, I probably had a glass of wine next to me, and I was looking for interesting phrases in social psychology articles. I had 12 tabs open, when I found, in a footnote, a brief precis of the black bag experiment (University of Oregon, 1967). It struck me as beautiful and ridiculous. I wasn’t really interested in the findings of the experiment, which focused more on others’ gradually more affectionate reactions to black bag over time. What obsessed me was the experience of portraying black bag: what kind of actor would leap at the chance to do it? The fact that it was a pretty neat symbol of the status of the artist in the 21st century … The fact that I wasn’t averse to the idea of doing it myself because, ugh, just being a person at all is so wearying.

It was a really lucky and completely arbitrary find and I felt utterly rejuvenated by it as a concept. I like writing that has some kind of constraint (like Georges Perec’s novel A Void, composed without a single letter “e”), a rule that starts to generate the work; that becomes its own inspiration. But this was a constraint for a character within the book, and that struck me as even better. Within minutes of reading about it I felt like I was black bag, my constant inner monologue turned into even more of a bathysphere than usual.

I immediately abandoned the poem I was working on and started writing a first-person scene where an out-of-work actor talks to a psychology lecturer about the role of black bag. It was pretty much all I wrote from that point on. I wrote BLACK BAG on the front of a notebook and vowed to do as little research as possible.

M John Harrison The End of Everything

I always start writing from an interest in form, rather than from ideas for characters or scenes or stories. They come later. As soon as I find the form, I look for its weak points so I can break it. The two forms that interested me when I began to think about The End of Everything were the UK novel of catastrophe after the second world war, expressed best in John Wyndham’s The Day of the Triffids and its outbreak of ambulatory carnivorous vegetables; and the novel of the alien invasion of Earth epitomised by HG Wells’s classic The War of the Worlds.

In both, the disaster is bounded, understandable and, most importantly, solved. This is not necessarily true of disasters in the real world; they’re constant, unmanageable, entangled with one another and with global politics; and wherever possible they go unacknowledged by people whose comforts are not immediately threatened. The classic disaster stories burst in on a fictional population, rag it about, and then, having taught the reader a lesson, recede. They encourage us to feel good by presenting unpredictable upheaval followed briskly by the defeat of the threat and a return to some form of the author’s preferred cultural ground state.

I wanted this book to offer a different shape: a catastrophe the nature of which is impossible to parse, and which continues unabated for the foreseeable future. In short, actual change. Nested inside the novel are various parodies, pastiches and political metaphors; a certain amount of grotesque humour. The End of Everything is about trying to live as if nothing has gone wrong. It’s a disaster story in which the disaster is the failure to comprehend. It’s an alien invasion narrative in which the aliens arrive not as Wells’s invaders from Mars but as incomers from another dimension, paralleling the gentrification of places like the UK’s south-east coast. Their motives are so unhuman that we aren’t sure even they know how – or why – they came.

As a favour – and with a whispered You’re welcome! Enjoy! – I’ve passed on to the reader some of the puzzlement and confusion of the characters in the book as they face a future with the alien. I hope, though, that the issues are transparent: the collapse of rationality that comes with Trumpism and the internet, and which consciously confounds the ability to make a factual statement about anything; humanity’s inexplicable attempt to break down and abandon the environment it can’t live without; the loss of any sense that we actually know how to manage the world except via a Netflix empowerment fantasy.

In an early film of The Day of the Triffids, the triffids are defeated by spraying salt water on them; in the novel itself, the hero and his dependents ignore the issue of giant carnivorous plants and retreat to the Isle of Wight, where they return to the ground state by starting an allotment. We don’t have those options.

GeneralTab.title: Tens of thousands of tents flooded after heavy rains in Gaza
GeneralTab.text:
Heavy rains have flooded tens of thousands of tents where displaced residents have been living in Gaza, with a United Nations official saying almost everyone in the territory needs help.

Residents used pots and pans to clear water from their flooded tents, with some saying they were left without shelter.

Jonathan Veitch, the Unicef representative for Palestine, said the "desperate" situation was being made worse by Israeli restrictions on the entry of heavy machinery and supplies such as engine oil.

Some 90% of Gaza residents have been displaced by the Israeli war against Hamas, many of them multiple times, with limited access to clean water and sanitation.

Aid agencies say the situation is likely to worsen with the start of the rainy season.

Speaking to the BBC from Deir Al Balah in central Gaza, Veitch said: "It's just horrific and they're absolutely desperate.

"We're providing all the assistance that we can but we're getting stopped on the street as we're driving now because people are begging us for help."

The Hamas-run government in Gaza said about 70,000 tents had been flooded. A spokesperson said the "collapse of dozens of cracked walls and roofs" had caused injuries, some of which were critical.

Veitch also said there were fewer tarpaulins, plastic sheeting and tents available in the Gaza strip due to UN budget cuts.

"We have to be much more choosy about where we're going to be supporting," he said.

"But unfortunately, heavy flooding this morning means that nearly everyone needs help."

Israel has said it restricts the entry of items into Gaza that could be used for military purposes.

Maryam Odeh, 34, who lives with her children in Deir al-Balah, told AFP news agency: "We no longer know how to protect our children.

"My children ask me where we will sleep tonight, and I have no answer."

Khaled al-Najjar, 41, told AFP: "We fear for our children not only from the flooding of the tents, but also from the cold and the widespread diseases."

GeneralTab.title: Victims in rape cases must not feel like they are on trial, Burnham says
GeneralTab.text:
Andy Burnham has said the government needs to make sure that victims in rape cases do not feel like they are on trial.

His comments come after Metropolitan Police boss Sir Mark Rowley told the BBC that what he heard reported from Russell Brand's trial came very close to "victim blaming".

The government needs to "constantly look" at how rape trials are conducted to better support alleged victims in court, the prime minister told Times Radio, although BBC News understands there are no plans to change the law around rape trials.

Actor and comedian Brand was found guilty of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault after a four-week trial in London.

During an interview with BBC Radio 4's Today programme on Friday, it was put to Sir Mark that Brand's defence barrister Ian Winter KC "told jurors none of the complainants had in his words 'resisted, screamed or even tried to leave'".

Sir Mark replied: "I think what I've heard reported heads towards, it's getting very close to victim blaming, which is something we've thought very hard about in policing and make sure we don't do."

He said he would support a call from the Victims' Commissioner for a legal duty that would require judges to direct juries on rape myths and misconceptions in every rape trial.

"It shouldn't be possible for inaccurate statements to be made to a jury to suggest that because a rape victim didn't behave in one way that somehow undermines their case," Sir Mark explained.

In a Times Radio interview on Saturday, Burnham said he would "look closely" at the police chief's comments.

He said the government needed to look at how to "make sure they do not leave the woman feeling like she is on trial in court".

"[I'm] always prepared to make changes," he said. "We need to encourage more women to come forward to report rape, we need to get the conviction rate up.

"All of this is part of our broader agenda as a government combatting violence against women and girls."

Pressed on whether this might lead to a change in the law, the prime minister replied: "I wouldn't rule anything out... I will study what's happened here in great detail."

Brand, who has starred in films including Forgetting Sarah Marshall, will be sentenced on Monday and is expected to face substantial jail time.

He was found not guilty of two other counts of rape, and one count of attempted indecent assault after the jury deliberated for eight-and-a-half hours.

The 51-year-old was refused bail and will spend the weekend in custody.

It has since been revealed that Brand is also facing further rape allegations made by two women and has been questioned by officers in relation to the complaints. The Met said its investigation "remains ongoing".

Sir Mark told BBC Breakfast he "wouldn't be surprised if many more came forward".

In the wake of Brand's trial, Victims' Commissioner Claire Waxman said rape trials must be conducted "in a way that challenges myths and misconceptions about sexual violence".

In a social media post, Waxman wrote that "victims need confidence that the justice process is fair and based on evidence, not myths and false assumptions about rape and trauma".

Speaking to the Today programme on Saturday, director and founder of the Centre for Women's Justice Harriet Wistrich agreed that juries need to understand "underlying behaviours" without "running to judgement" over how a victim behaved in a particular way.

But former Conservative MP Anna Soubry, who has now returned to her work as a barrister where she often defends rape and sexual offence cases in the Crown court, told the BBC "people are being misled" by Sir Mark's comments.

"Every single judge in those cases must give, and does give, a very firm direction to the jury on exactly these points," she said.

As a result, she said she was " really disappointed" in the police chief and stressed "we've got to trust our juries" who are able to have an understanding of the nature of sexual offences.

GeneralTab.title: Three held after boy hurt in sword attack near Gloucester school
GeneralTab.text:
Two menand a boyhave been arrested after a teenager was injured in an attack involving a sword near two schools in Gloucester.

St Peter's High School and Willow Primary Academy, in Tuffley, were put into lockdown after the incident at 08:50 GMT on Friday.

Police said a 17-year-old suffered a wound "believed to have been caused by the sword".

A 19-year-old was arrested overnight on suspicion of assault occasioning actual bodily harm and affray. An 18-year-old was held on suspicion of possession of an offensive weapon, assault occasioning actual bodily harm and affray. Meanwhile another 17-year-old boy was arrested on suspicion of assisting an offender.

The trio - who are all from Gloucester - remain in police custody for questioning.

Two men, one with a sword, had been seen chasing two boys, according to police on Friday.

Armed officers attended the scene to search for the suspects who reportedly fled on foot.

Police said the 17-year-old suffered a "superficial wound believed to have been caused by the sword".

The other boy involved was not injured.
